examples.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
y' - 6 y = 9 e ^ {6 x}.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is $y_c(x) = Ae^{6x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.
examples.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution $y_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
y_c' - 6 y_c=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c = A e^{6x}.
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution $y_p(x).$

We see that the right-hand side is $9 e ^ {6 x},$ and $e^{6x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
y_p = \alpha x  e ^ {6x} ,
$$

where $\alpha$ is a constant to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of $y_p$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{6x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{6x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{6x}+6x{e}^{6x}) \\  & =\alpha (1+6x){e}^{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha,$ we substitute $y_p$ and $y_p'$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1+6x){e}^{6x})-6\alpha x{e}^{6x} & =9{e}^{6x} \\ (1+6x-6x)\alpha {e}^{6x} & =9{e}^{6x} \\ \alpha {e}^{6x} & =9{e}^{6x} \\ \alpha  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution $y_p(x)$ is

$$
y_p(x) = 9x  e ^ {6 x} .
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x) = y_c(x)+y_p(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y =  Ae^{6x} + 9xe^{6x}.
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $6{e}^{-3x}+10{e}^{2x},$ and ${e}^{-3x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, while ${e}^{2x}$ is not, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-3x}+\beta {e}^{2x},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-3x}+\beta {e}^{2x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-3x})^{′}+\beta ({e}^{2x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-3x}-3x{e}^{-3x})+2\beta {e}^{2x} \\  & =\alpha (1-3x){e}^{-3x}+2\beta {e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1-3x){e}^{-3x}+2\beta {e}^{2x})+3(\alpha x{e}^{-3x}+\beta {e}^{2x}) & =6{e}^{-3x}+10{e}^{2x} \\ (1-3x+3x)\alpha {e}^{-3x}+(2\beta +3\beta ){e}^{2x} & =6{e}^{-3x}+10{e}^{2x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-3x}+5\beta {e}^{2x} & =6{e}^{-3x}+10{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients of ${e}^{-3x}$ and ${e}^{2x}$ gives

$$
\alpha =6\,\text{and}\,5\beta =10,
$$

so, we have

$$
\alpha =6\,\text{and}\,\beta =2.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=6x{e}^{-3x}+2{e}^{2x}.
$$
